newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Nigerian council polls test of move to democracy.
newsitem.headline: Nigerian council polls test of move to democracy.

text.p: Nigeria holds local council elections this weekend that will be seen as a test of the military government's commitment to restoring democracy.
Electioneering is in full swing for Saturday's poll with rallies and posters promising a better life. Voters will choose councillors for more than 1,000 local government areas nationwide.

"The fact, however, is that the real issue in this election is how serious and how sincere the military government is about its transition to civil rule," said Emas Adaku, a political commentator in the central Nigerian city of Jos.
"If the election is successfully carried out they will be beating their chests this time next week that they are on the right path to democracy," he added.

The election, rescheduled from the last quarter of last year, will be the first on a multi-party basis since the annulment of a June 12, 1993 presidential poll which had been expected to restore democracy to Nigeria.
The last voting, held on a non-party basis last March, saw a massive turnout. Politicians believe voter turnout should be equally heavy this time following registration of five political parties.
The parties will be testing their strength ahead of voting for state governors later this year and a presidential vote next year.

The opposition has not called for a boycott but has restated its view that military ruler General Sani Abacha's promise to hand over to a democratically-elected government on October 1, 1998 is a ruse. Many believe Abacha will seek election as president himself.

"Our view remains that only a government of national unity headed by Chief Abiola can end the current political impasse and lead to a genuine restoration of democracy," said Moses Adebiyi, a spokesman for the umbrella opposition group NADECO.
Abiola, a rich businessman, is presumed to have won the annulled vote but has been jailed since June 1994 when he proclaimed himself president in defiance of Abacha.
"Abiola's detention and failure to resolve the issue of his mandate hang like an albatross over the nation," wrote Ayodele Akinkuotu of the opposition Tell magazine in this week's issue.
But many in Abacha's government regard the issue of the annulled election as dead and point to relative peace, despite a recent spate of bomb blasts believed linked to the political crisis.
Western diplomats will be monitoring the polls to see if Nigeria is actually democratising as touted by the military rulers and their civilian supporters.
Nigeria fell from favour with Western nations over the 1993 annulment, which unleashed mayhem in the populous African nation and paved way for Abacha to seize power later that year.

Relations with the West worsened after the 1995 hanging of nine minority rights activists including author Ken Saro-Wiwa from the Ogoni tribe, who were tried by a tribunal for the murder of four pro-government Ogoni chiefs.

Nigeria remains a pariah over the lack of democracy and alleged human rights abuses and is expected to be in the dock at the six-week session of the United Nations human rights commission that began in Geneva on Monday.
But the government insists it is on the way to civil rule and foreign criticism is interference in the country's internal affairs.

"They keep talking about democracy, democracy. Even if we elect Mr Right with the blessing of every Nigerian, so long as we don't toe their line we are Mr Bad," said Mamman Nasir, chairman of the committee overseeing the transition programme.
